prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "AngloGold Ashanti PLC" (ticker AU). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: AngloGold Ashanti shows price momentum over the past year (up about 27%), but it sells an undifferentiated commodity in a centuries-old industry, with no brand advantage or emerging-industry leadership. It meets very few of Gardner's Rule Breaker traits.
summaries.buffett: Buffett avoids commodity producers whose earnings depend on prices they cannot set, and AngloGold's results swung from a $235M loss in 2023 to $2,636M of net income in 2025 almost entirely on the gold price. Its balance sheet is now strong, but there is no durable moat or predictable earnings stream.
summaries.munger: Munger would see AngloGold as a hard business: a price taker with depleting assets, high capital needs and operations in risky jurisdictions. Inverting, a lower gold price, cost inflation, safety incidents or resource nationalism could each sharply cut its value.
summaries.lynch: AngloGold is a classic Lynch cyclical, and its trailing P/E of about 12.5 looks low because earnings sit near a peak from record gold prices, which Lynch warned is when cyclicals are most dangerous. Its share count rose about 7.7% in a year after the Centamin deal, and there is no sign of insider buying.
summaries.fisher: Fisher's points on new products, R&D and sales skill hardly apply to a gold miner; AngloGold competes on costs and ore bodies, not innovation. Management's Full Asset Potential cost programme shows some operational discipline but not the growth culture Fisher sought.
summaries.graham: AngloGold fails Graham's defensive tests: it lost money in 2015 and 2023, its dividend was suspended for years in the mid-2010s, and the price is about 40 times three-year average earnings. P/E times P/B of about 67 is far above Graham's 22.5 limit.
summaries.thiel: AngloGold has no proprietary technology or monopoly; gold mining is a competitive commodity business. Its long-life ore bodies are valuable but not the kind of 10x technology advantage Thiel looks for.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner seeks secular growth compounders, and AngloGold's growth is a function of the gold price rather than of rising demand for a product it controls. It can be a macro or hedge position but does not match his growth framework.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller has publicly favoured gold at times as a hedge against monetary debasement, and AngloGold is a leveraged way to express that view: free cash flow nearly tripled to about $1.2B in Q1 2026. But the shares are about 29% below their 52-week high of $129, so the price trend has weakened.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids mining companies because they lack pricing power and their returns are cyclical. AngloGold's current ROIC of about 45% reflects record gold prices rather than a durable, high-return franchise.
summaries.greenblatt: On current numbers AngloGold scores well on the Magic Formula: EV/EBIT of about 7.8 (an earnings yield near 13%) and return on capital of about 45%. Greenblatt would note that these figures are at a cyclical peak and may not last.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs an extraordinary business, skilled management and great reinvestment opportunities; AngloGold has competent management but a commodity business with depleting assets. It does not fit his approach.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai buys simple businesses at deep discounts in temporary distress; AngloGold was distressed in 2023 but is now enjoying record profits. Its low-debt balance sheet limits downside, but there is no Dhandho-style mispricing today.
summaries.wood: AngloGold has no exposure to ARK's innovation platforms such as AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomics. It falls outside Cathie Wood's framework.
summaries.ackman: Ackman's criteria call for simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with pricing power and high barriers to entry. AngloGold's free cash flow is large now ($4.47B TTM) but unpredictable, and it has no pricing power.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep looked for businesses that share scale benefits with customers and become harder to compete with over time; a gold miner selling at the spot price cannot do that. Its position in 10-20 years depends on replacing reserves rather than on strengthening a moat.
summaries.valentine: Valentine wanted huge markets and products that solve painful problems; AngloGold sells a store-of-value metal in a mature market. It does not fit his framework.

momentum.evidence: AU rose about 27.4% in the 52 weeks to October 13, 2026 ($91.65), ahead of the S&P 500 (SPY total return about 20.4%), but it is about 29% below its 52-week high of $129.

g4.evidence: CEO Alberto Calderon (since 2021) has improved results, but the company is not backed by well-known star investors.

g6.evidence: Analysts generally see AU as cheap, at about 10 times forward earnings, rather than overvalued.

simple.evidence: AngloGold mines gold and sells it at the market price, a business that is easy to understand even if mining is technically complex.

b2.evidence: Revenue was $4,595M in 2020, fell to $4,029M in 2021 and jumped to $9,893M in 2025, and it lost $235M in 2023.

integrity.evidence: Management pays out about half of free cash flow as dividends and moved to a NYSE primary listing with UK domicile, but it issued shares for Centamin and has faced safety and community controversies.

b6.evidence: The 2024 Centamin acquisition added the Sukari mine and fits the core strategy, but it diluted shareholders by about 7.7% in share count over the past year.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 45% now with little debt ($1.79B against $2.78B cash), but returns were negative in 2023 and depend on the gold price.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was $3,335M in 2025 and $4,471M on a trailing basis, above net income of $3,807M.

b10.evidence: Over the past decade much retained capital went into mines that later lost money or were sold, and the 2023 loss shows retained earnings did not compound steadily.

safety.evidence: At about 10 times forward earnings the price looks cheap, but only if gold stays near current record levels.

fairprice.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 12.5 and FCF yield of about 9.5% look reasonable, but they rest on peak gold prices.

mu5.evidence: A lower gold price, cost inflation (Q1 2026 AISC up nearly 20% to about $1,955/oz), safety incidents and resource nationalism in Africa are many ways to lose value.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in Nevada and Colombian projects, but mining returns are cyclical and assets deplete.

ly2.evidence: AngloGold is a clear cyclical whose story is higher gold prices plus cost control and Sukari's contribution.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 12.5 is below recent earnings growth, but that growth comes from gold prices and is unlikely to repeat.

runway.evidence: Production is roughly flat at about 3.1Moz a year; sales growth depends on gold prices, not on new markets.

ly7.evidence: The share count rose about 7.7% in a year after the Centamin deal, and there is no record of significant insider buying.

ly8.evidence: Gold mining is an out-of-favour niche for many generalists, though AU is well covered by mining analysts.

fi2.evidence: As a gold miner it does not develop new products; it develops new mines such as the Nevada Beatty district.

fi3.evidence: Exploration spending has added reserves in Nevada and Colombia, but there is no clear R&D programme to judge.

fi4.evidence: Gold is sold at the spot price to refiners and banks, so selling skill is not a factor.

longterm.evidence: Management invests in long-life projects such as Nevada and Obuasi's redevelopment, but also returns about half of free cash flow each period.

gr1.evidence: AngloGold has a market value of about $46.8B and 2025 revenue of $9,893M, making it one of the largest gold miners.

ni10.evidence: It reported net losses in 2015 ($73M) and 2023 ($235M).

gr4.evidence: AngloGold suspended its dividend for several years in the mid-2010s to cut debt.

eps10.evidence: It went from a net loss of $73M in 2015 to net income of $2,636M ($5.18 a share) in 2025, though only because of record gold prices.

gr6.evidence: The price of $91.65 is about 40 times average EPS for 2023-2025 (-$0.56, $2.33, $5.18).

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 12.5 times a P/B of about 5.3 gives about 67, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: It has no proprietary technology; mining methods are similar across peers.

timing.evidence: Central-bank buying and investment demand have pushed gold to records (Q1 2026 realised price $4,863/oz, up 69%), making the current timing very favourable.

th3.evidence: It is a long-established miner in a mature global market, not a company that started by dominating a small niche.

team.evidence: Alberto Calderon, a Yale economics PhD and former BHP and Orica executive, has delivered strong results but is not an exceptional founder.

th5.evidence: Gold needs no sales effort since refiners and banks buy all it produces, so distribution is not a differentiator.

durable.evidence: Long-life ore bodies like Geita, Sukari and Kibali will last years, but each mine depletes and must be replaced.

th7.evidence: Its opportunity is the same gold price exposure all miners share.

trend.evidence: It benefits from the strong gold cycle driven by central-bank buying, but not from AI or cloud computing.

dr1.evidence: TTM EPS rose to $7.46 from $5.18 in 2025, and Q1 2026 free cash flow of about $1.2B was a record.

dr2.evidence: Higher gold prices and Sukari help, but rising costs and Obuasi problems could offset them.

dr4.evidence: Central-bank gold buying, geopolitical tension and expectations of easier monetary policy support gold prices.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include record dividends (116 cents a share in Q1 2026), Nevada project progress and Q3 2026 results.

dr7.evidence: Dependence on the gold price, jurisdiction risk and operational problems argue against a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is about 55% now but was 23% in 2023, reflecting gold prices rather than pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: Free-cash-flow yield is about 9.5% ($4.47B TTM FCF on a $46.8B market value).

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 7.8, an operating earnings yield of about 13%.

pa2.evidence: Gold miners are at a cyclical peak, not in a temporary setback.

pa4.evidence: Net cash limits balance-sheet risk, but a lower gold price could cut the share price sharply and permanently for buyers at peak prices.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics.

wo2.evidence: Its costs are rising, not falling (AISC about $1,955/oz in Q1 2026).

wo3.evidence: It does not combine any ARK-style innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Gold demand will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Its results depend almost entirely on the gold price and on input costs such as fuel and labour.

ns1.evidence: As a price taker it cannot pass scale savings to customers to build a moat.

ns4.evidence: Its position in 10-20 years depends on replacing reserves at depleting mines and is not clearly stronger than today.

va2.evidence: Gold serves as a store of value and is used in jewellery and electronics, but it does not solve a large, painful problem for most people.
